beats.say: A penny gets you a record. The bill arrives later.
Sign up, get twelve albums for a penny.
Then you must buy a set number of albums at regular price.
Ignore the deadline, and the next album ships with a full-price invoice.
Revenue hit $1.4 billion in 1996, then $17 million by 2014. Sounds impossible.
But it does a job: a negative-option trap.
The required-purchase clause forces a future bill.
Peak revenue proves the trap; the crash proves its cost.
A gym offers a $1 trial, then auto-renews at $49 month.
The $1 lure makes the $49 plan feel reasonable.
Spot hidden commitments behind tiny offers. Follow for more.
